title: Homage and refuge at dawn
hookLine: the morning chant of Theravada monasteries: homage, refuges, reflections
carry: going for refuge, in one shared tongue

lines: A WOODEN BELL IN THE DARK.
ONE LINE, THEN ALL OF THEM.
cards: It's still dark. A wooden bell sounds across a monastery courtyard, and figures in robes cross to the hall, barefoot, carrying small lights.

They kneel in rows facing a Buddha image, laypeople from the village behind them. Someone in front draws a breath and sings out a single line, and the whole room picks it up, low and even, like a river finding its bed.
Nobody looks at a page. A new block begins today, the practice traditions, with the sound that opens the day.

teach.b: In the order heard in some Theravada monasteries, the morning chant moves in three steps. First, homage: "Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa."
Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the fully self-awakened one.

By custom it's said three times, slowly, and it names the Buddha by three qualities, not by a personal name. Second, the refuges: "Buddham saranam gacchami. Dhammam saranam gacchami. Sangham saranam gacchami."
To the Buddha I go for refuge, to the teaching, to the community. Then again, opening with dutiyampi, a second time, and with tatiyampi, a third.
You met the three jewels earlier this year; here they are in the mouth, before breakfast. Third, the reflections.
Chanting books vary from monastery to monastery, but a common one comes from the Buddha's own advice in the Numerical Discourses: five facts to recall often. I am subject to aging.
I am subject to illness. I am subject to death. I will be parted from everyone and everything dear to me.
My actions are my own, and I will inherit them. It sounds heavy for the morning. Some teachers say the opposite: it makes the day lighter, because nothing in it comes as a surprise.
Why Pali, if the room speaks Thai or Sinhala or Burmese? These are the words the tradition has kept, and a monk from Sri Lanka and a nun from Thailand can chant them together without a translator.

how: In Theravada monasteries, monks, nuns and lay visitors chant in Pali at morning and evening services, opening with homage to the Buddha said three times, then the three refuges, then reflections, often from memory.

o: a silent reading from the Pali canon before breakfast
a song in Thai that monks sing to wake the village
the Theravada morning chant: homage, refuges and reflections

games.q: the morning chant: tap the pairs.

s: the homage names the Buddha by his personal name
it names him by three qualities: the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the fully self-awakened one.
the refuges are chanted a second and a third time
the chant repeats them, opening with dutiyampi and tatiyampi.
the morning reflections avoid aging, illness and death
the five facts to recall name all three, plus parting from what is dear and owning one's actions.

games.q: you're a nun from Thailand visiting a monastery in Sri Lanka. you don't speak Sinhala. the morning chant begins. what happens?
o: you sit silently, unable to join.
you chant along, because it's in Pali.
games.why: the chant is in Pali, so monks and nuns from different countries can chant together without a translator.

practice: Whether you're a Buddhist or just learning the sound, say the homage slowly, on one breath if you can, three times: namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa.

If you'd like, add the refuges: Buddham saranam gacchami, Dhammam saranam gacchami, Sangham saranam gacchami. Don't worry about every syllable; let the rhythm carry you, then sit in the quiet the chant leaves behind.
